items.title: Multiplayer AI Manifesto
items.summary:
The Multiplayer AI Manifesto: a vision for the future of AI at organizations.

Today, most people work with AI agents in a fundamentally single-player way. The siloed, local nature of AI chats has real costs to organizations, which I explain.

My team and I have been working in a fundamentally multiplayer way for over a year. Anyone on the team can join anyone else's Claude/Codex/Pi/etc session. Any agent session can be resumed with full context, months later. Code is never checked out locally, and editors are never opened.

In working this way, and in talking with many companies undergoing their own AI transformations, I wrote up a vision of what true multiplayer AI should entail.

Here it is, in five principles, with associated motivations, potential misconceptions, and important considerations.

Never copy-and-paste
Work with the door open
Continuously improve
People are not routers
Nothing starts from scratch
Full text with the diagrams: https://multiplayer-ai.com

items.title: Building Europe's AI Stack — Inside the Barcelona Supercomputing Center

We sat down with the Barcelona Supercomputing Center to talk about what it really takes to turn a continent's scientific ambition into an AI powerhouse.

The model is simple in concept, hard to execute: energy → chips → infrastructure → models → applications. Five layers. One coherent stack.

items.title: How Many Narrow AIs Could Behave Like One Superintelligence - Daniel Kokotajlo and Thomas Larsen
items.summary:
Could slowing AI development make superintelligence safer? Daniel Kokotajlo and Thomas Larsen of the AI Futures Project join Tim Scarfe to examine AI 2040: Plan A, a proposal to buy time before AI exceeds human control.

SPONSOR:
---
Cyber Fund built the Monastery to help founders ship products that were impossible a year ago.
Apply now: https://cyber.fund
---

After revisiting AI 2027 and the limits of forecasting, they ask what happens when AI can automate research and sustain an economy without human workers. Tim challenges the case for general models and asks whether intelligence alone explains power. Plan A proposes an initial pause to build safety infrastructure, then cautious development up to the strongest AI that can still be reliably controlled. The discussion tests the distinction between control and alignment, the case for public AI research, and whether the US and China could enforce a slowdown. It ends with the evidence that would change their forecasts.
